The isothermal process follows the isotherm, on which pressure times volume is constant. The adiabatic process starts at the same point but falls more steeply than the isotherm, because no energy is transferred thermally. Illustrative data.

Only whole forces are drawn: the weight appears once, and its components along and across the slope are not drawn beside it. The four forces add to zero, which is why the block stays at rest. precalc-hole.title: A hole in a rational function
precalc-hole.subtitle: The limit exists from both sides, but the function is not defined there
precalc-hole.caption: r(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) simplifies to x + 2 everywhere except x = 2, where it is undefined. Inputs close to 2 give outputs close to 4, so the hole is at (2, 4), drawn as an open circle.
precalc-hole.alt: A straight line rising from lower left to upper right, with a single open circle at the point two comma four. The function is a rational expression whose numerator and denominator share a factor, so it equals x plus two everywhere except at x equals two, where it is undefined. Inputs just below and just above two both give outputs arbitrarily close to four, so the limit from each side is four and the hole sits at the point two comma four. The circle is drawn open, not filled, because the function does not take that value: a filled dot would say the opposite.
precalc-hole.note: Open circle: the limit is 4, but r(2) does not exist.
labels: The hole sits at that point
covers: The hole sits at that point

used_by.title: Location of a hole
used_by.contract_note: AP Precalculus 1.10 is a formula entry with no authored items[]; the two-sided limit, the point the hole sits at, and the function being undefined there are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b). The entry's formula states exactly that chain.

precalc-transformations-additive.title: Additive transformations translate the graph
precalc-transformations-additive.subtitle: f(x) + k moves it vertically; f(x + h) moves it horizontally by −h
precalc-transformations-additive.caption: The parent f(x) = 0.5x² with two additive transformations. Adding 3 to the OUTPUT lifts the graph three units. Adding −2 to the INPUT moves it two units to the right — the opposite direction to the sign, which is the part students misread.
precalc-transformations-additive.alt: Three parabolas. The solid one is the parent function, one half x squared, with its vertex at the origin. One dashed curve is the same shape lifted three units, which is the parent with three added to its output. The other dashed curve is the same shape moved two units to the RIGHT, which is the parent with minus two added to its input. A change to the output moves the graph the way the sign reads; a change to the input moves it the opposite way, so adding a negative number inside shifts right rather than left.
precalc-transformations-additive.note: Inside the function, the shift goes the OPPOSITE way to the sign.

precalc-transformations-multiplicative.title: Multiplicative transformations stretch and reflect
precalc-transformations-multiplicative.subtitle: a f(x) scales vertically; f(bx) scales horizontally by 1/b
precalc-transformations-multiplicative.caption: The same parent with two multiplicative transformations. Multiplying the OUTPUT by −1 reflects the graph over the x-axis. Multiplying the INPUT by 2 compresses it horizontally by a factor of one half — again the reciprocal, not the factor itself.
precalc-transformations-multiplicative.alt: Three curves sharing a vertex at the origin. The solid one is the parent, one half x squared. One dashed curve is its mirror image below the horizontal axis, which is the parent multiplied by minus one: a vertical dilation with a reflection. The other dashed curve is much narrower than the parent, which is the parent with its input multiplied by two: a horizontal dilation by a factor of one half. A factor applied to the output scales the graph by that factor; a factor applied to the input scales it by the RECIPROCAL, so multiplying the input by two makes the graph half as wide, not twice as wide.
precalc-transformations-multiplicative.note: Inside the function, the factor acts as its RECIPROCAL.

precalc-degree-from-points.title: How many points fix a polynomial's degree
precalc-degree-from-points.subtitle: Four points with distinct inputs are modelled by a cubic — degree 3 or less
precalc-degree-from-points.caption: Four points with distinct x values, and the cubic through them. In general n + 1 points with distinct inputs are modelled by a polynomial of degree n or less: four points give degree 3 or less, not necessarily exactly 3.
precalc-degree-from-points.alt: Four marked points with distinct horizontal positions, at x equals minus one, zero, one and two, with a single smooth cubic curve passing through all four. Four points with distinct inputs determine a polynomial of degree three or less. Degree three OR LESS matters: if the four points happened to lie on a straight line, the polynomial through them would be degree one, and the count of points sets an upper bound on the degree rather than fixing it exactly.
precalc-degree-from-points.note: n + 1 points give degree n or LESS — an upper bound, not an exact degree.
labels: A polynomial of degree 3 or less fits them
covers: A polynomial of degree 3 or less fits them

used_by.title: Points determine polynomial degree
used_by.contract_note: AP Precalculus 1.13 is a convention with no authored items[]; the four distinct inputs and the degree-3-or-less polynomial through them are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b), which is the entry's body with n = 3.

precalc-sequence.title: A sequence is a function on the whole numbers
precalc-sequence.subtitle: Its graph is a set of points, not a curve
precalc-sequence.caption: The sequence aₙ = 2n + 1 for n = 0 to 6. The graph is seven separate points. There is nothing between them to draw: the sequence has no value at n = 1.5.
precalc-sequence.alt: Seven separate dots rising steadily from left to right, at horizontal positions zero through six and heights one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven and thirteen. This is the graph of a sequence, which is a function whose inputs are the whole numbers. The dots are not joined, because the sequence has no value between consecutive whole numbers: there is no term at n equals one and a half. Drawing a line through them would assert values the sequence does not have, which is the difference between a sequence and a function on the real numbers. The graph is therefore discrete.
precalc-sequence.note: Not joined: there is no term between consecutive whole numbers.
labels: The graph is a set of discrete points
covers: The graph is a set of discrete points

precalc-exponential-shape.entry_title: Shape and extrema of exponential functions
precalc-exponential-shape.title: The shape of an exponential function
precalc-exponential-shape.subtitle: Always increasing or always decreasing, always one way concave, and no extremum
precalc-exponential-shape.caption: f(x) = 2ˣ. It rises everywhere, bends upwards everywhere, and never turns: an exponential has no maximum, no minimum and no point of inflection, and its graph approaches the x-axis without reaching it.
precalc-exponential-shape.alt: The graph of two to the power x, rising from near zero on the left to eight on the right. It increases at every point and is concave up at every point, so it never turns around and never changes the direction of its bend. That is why an exponential function has no maximum, no minimum and no point of inflection, except that a maximum and minimum do exist if you restrict it to a closed interval, where they occur at the endpoints. The dashed line at y equals zero is a horizontal asymptote: the curve approaches it without ever reaching it.
precalc-exponential-shape.note: Extrema only on a closed interval, and then only at its endpoints.
labels: No extremum and no point of inflection
covers: No extremum and no point of inflection

used_by.title: Shape and extrema of exponential functions
used_by.contract_note: AP Precalculus 2.3 is a convention with no authored items[]; monotonicity, a single concavity and the absence of extrema or inflection are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b), and the entry's body lists exactly those three.

precalc-log-reflection.entry_title: Graph and ordered pairs of log vs. exponential
precalc-log-reflection.title: A logarithm is its exponential reflected over y = x
precalc-log-reflection.subtitle: If (s, t) lies on bˣ then (t, s) lies on logᵇ x
precalc-log-reflection.caption: f(x) = 2ˣ and g(x) = log₂ x, with the line y = x between them. Each curve is the other's mirror image in that line, so every ordered pair on one appears with its coordinates swapped on the other: (1, 2) on the exponential becomes (2, 1) on the logarithm.
precalc-log-reflection.alt: Two curves and a straight diagonal line. The steeply rising curve is two to the power x; the slowly rising one is the logarithm base two of x; the diagonal is the line y equals x. The two curves are mirror images of each other in that diagonal. Reflecting a point over y equals x swaps its coordinates, so a point at one comma two on the exponential corresponds to a point at two comma one on the logarithm. That is what makes the two functions inverses: the exponential's outputs are the logarithm's inputs and the other way round. The logarithm is drawn only for positive inputs, because that is its whole domain.
precalc-log-reflection.note: Reflecting over y = x swaps the coordinates: (s, t) becomes (t, s).
labels: Each is the other's reflection over y = x
The logarithm is defined only for positive inputs
covers: Each is the other's reflection over y = x
The logarithm is defined only for positive inputs

used_by.title: Graph and ordered pairs of log vs. exponential
used_by.contract_note: AP Precalculus 2.10 is a convention with no authored items[]; the reflection, the swapped ordered pair and the logarithm's positive domain are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b). The entry's body states the first two; the third is why only half the plane carries a logarithm and is drawn.

precalc-sinusoid-concavity.title: A sinusoid alternates concavity
precalc-sinusoid-concavity.subtitle: Concave down over each crest, concave up over each trough
precalc-sinusoid-concavity.caption: y = sin x over two full periods. Between 0 and π the graph is concave down; between π and 2π it is concave up; and the pattern repeats. The bend flips at every point where the curve crosses its midline.
precalc-sinusoid-concavity.alt: The sine curve drawn over two full periods, from zero to four pi. Over the first hump, between zero and pi, the graph is concave down: it bends downwards throughout, even while it is rising on the way up to the crest. Between pi and two pi it is concave up, bending upwards throughout. The pattern then repeats. The concavity changes exactly where the curve crosses its midline, at zero, pi, two pi, three pi and four pi, and those crossings are the points of inflection. Rising and falling is not the same as concave up and down: the curve is rising and concave down on the first quarter period.
precalc-sinusoid-concavity.note: The bend flips at each midline crossing — those are the inflection points.

used_by.title: Concavity of sinusoidal graphs
used_by.contract_note: AP Precalculus 3.5 is a convention with no authored items[]; the concavity over a crest, over a trough, and the alternation as x increases are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b), which is the entry's body.

precalc-tangent-reflections.title: A negative coefficient reflects the tangent graph
precalc-tangent-reflections.subtitle: a tan θ with a < 0 is the graph reflected over the x-axis
precalc-tangent-reflections.caption: y = tan θ and y = −tan θ on one pair of axes. The negative outside coefficient reflects the graph over the x-axis. A negative coefficient INSIDE, tan(bθ) with b < 0, reflects over the y-axis instead — which for tangent gives the same curve, because tangent is an odd function.
precalc-tangent-reflections.alt: Two sets of tangent branches between vertical dashed asymptotes. The solid branches rise from bottom left to top right between consecutive asymptotes; the dashed branches are their mirror image in the horizontal axis, falling instead of rising. That mirror image is y equals minus tangent theta: a negative coefficient outside the function reflects the graph over the x-axis. A negative coefficient inside, as in tangent of b theta with b negative, reflects over the y-axis instead; for tangent those two reflections happen to produce the same curve, because tangent is an odd function, so minus tangent theta and tangent of minus theta are equal. The curves are broken at each asymptote rather than drawn through it, because the function has no value there.
precalc-tangent-reflections.note: For tangent the two reflections coincide: tan(−θ) = −tan θ.
labels: a < 0 reflects the graph over the x-axis
b < 0 reflects it over the y-axis
Vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero
covers: a < 0 reflects the graph over the x-axis
b < 0 reflects it over the y-axis
Vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero

used_by.title: Reflections in tangent transformations
used_by.contract_note: AP Precalculus 3.8 is a convention with no authored items[]; the two reflections are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b). Only a < 0 is drawn: b < 0 produces the same curve for tangent, so it is carried in the figure's text instead of drawn twice, which the protocol allows and which is more honest than two identical curves. The asymptotes are drawn because the reflection is unreadable without them.

precalc-secant-graph.entry_title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent
precalc-secant-graph.title: The secant graph
precalc-secant-graph.subtitle: Vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero, and no values between −1 and 1
precalc-secant-graph.caption: y = sec θ. It has a vertical asymptote wherever cos θ = 0, and its range is everything at or beyond 1 in each direction: no point of the graph lies strictly between −1 and 1.
precalc-secant-graph.alt: The secant graph, drawn as separate U-shaped branches between vertical dashed asymptotes. Each asymptote sits where the cosine is zero, because secant is one over cosine and dividing by zero has no value. Every branch opens away from the horizontal axis, and no part of the graph lies strictly between minus one and one: the range is everything at or below minus one together with everything at or above one. The branches are broken at the asymptotes rather than joined across them.

used_by.title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent

precalc-cosecant-graph.entry_title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent
precalc-cosecant-graph.title: The cosecant graph
precalc-cosecant-graph.subtitle: Vertical asymptotes where sine is zero, and the same excluded band
precalc-cosecant-graph.caption: y = csc θ. Its asymptotes sit where sin θ = 0 — at 0 and at every multiple of π — and like the secant it takes no value strictly between −1 and 1.
precalc-cosecant-graph.alt: The cosecant graph, drawn as separate U-shaped branches between vertical dashed asymptotes. The asymptotes sit where the sine is zero, which is at zero and at every multiple of pi, because cosecant is one over sine. As with the secant, no part of the graph lies strictly between minus one and one. The difference between the two is only where the asymptotes fall: the secant's are where cosine vanishes, the cosecant's where sine does, which is a quarter period apart.
precalc-cosecant-graph.note: Same excluded band as the secant; the asymptotes sit a quarter period away.

used_by.title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent

precalc-cotangent-graph.entry_title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent
precalc-cotangent-graph.title: The cotangent graph
precalc-cotangent-graph.subtitle: Asymptotes where tangent is zero, and decreasing between consecutive ones
precalc-cotangent-graph.caption: y = cot θ. Its asymptotes sit where tan θ = 0, and between any two consecutive asymptotes the graph falls the whole way — unlike the secant and cosecant, it takes every real value.
precalc-cotangent-graph.alt: The cotangent graph, drawn as separate branches between vertical dashed asymptotes. Each branch starts high on the left of its interval and falls steadily to low on the right, so the function is decreasing between consecutive asymptotes rather than turning. The asymptotes sit where the tangent is zero, which is at zero and at every multiple of pi. Unlike the secant and the cosecant there is no excluded band: a cotangent branch passes through every real value between its two asymptotes.
precalc-cotangent-graph.note: Decreasing between consecutive asymptotes, and no excluded range.

used_by.title: Graph features of secant, cosecant, and cotangent

calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-wide.title: The same function, seen at the usual scale
calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-wide.subtitle: At this window f(x) = x³ − 0.01x looks like it only ever rises
calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-wide.caption: f(x) = x³ − 0.01x over −2 ≤ x ≤ 2. At this scale the graph appears to rise steadily through the origin with no turning points at all. Nothing here suggests otherwise.
calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-wide.alt: The graph of x cubed minus one hundredth of x, drawn over the interval from minus two to two with the vertical axis running from about minus eight to eight. At this scale it looks exactly like a plain cubic rising steadily through the origin, with no flat part and no turning points. The behaviour near the origin is far too small to see: the whole feature is about eight ten-thousandths tall, which at this scale is thinner than the drawn line. A shape read off this picture alone would be wrong, and that is the point: a graph is evidence about a function rather than proof, so an estimate taken from one should be treated with care.

calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-zoom.title: The same function, zoomed in near the origin
calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-zoom.subtitle: The same function over a window 13 times narrower and 10,000 times finer
calcab-scale-hides-behaviour-zoom.caption: The identical function over −0.15 ≤ x ≤ 0.15, with the vertical axis ten thousand times finer. There are two turning points, at about x = ±0.058, and a stretch where the function decreases — none of which the wide view showed.

bio-chloroplast.entry_title: Chloroplast structure and where photosynthetic reactions occur
bio-chloroplast.title: Chloroplast: regions and where the reactions happen
bio-chloroplast.subtitle: Light reactions in the grana; carbon fixation in the stroma around them
bio-chloroplast.caption: A chloroplast drawn as regions rather than as an illustration. Inside the double envelope, stacks of thylakoids are the grana, where the light reactions occur; the fluid around them, inside the inner membrane, is the stroma, where the Calvin cycle fixes carbon.
bio-chloroplast.alt: A schematic chloroplast: a rounded double boundary, an outer and an inner membrane, enclosing a space. Inside that space sit four stacks of flattened discs. Each disc is a thylakoid and its membrane holds the chlorophyll, organised into two photosystems, along with the electron transport proteins; a stack of them is a granum, and the light reactions happen there. The fluid filling the rest of the space inside the inner membrane is the stroma, and that is where carbon fixation, the Calvin cycle, takes place. The two sets of reactions are therefore in different places: one in a membrane, one in the fluid around it, which is what this diagram is read for. Illustrative data.

bio-mitochondrion.entry_title: Mitochondrion: regions and functions in respiration
bio-mitochondrion.title: Mitochondrion: regions and what happens in each
bio-mitochondrion.subtitle: Krebs cycle in the matrix; the gradient across the folded inner membrane
bio-mitochondrion.caption: A mitochondrion drawn as regions. The inner membrane folds into cristae, which is what gives it more area than the outer one and so more ATP synthase. The matrix inside it holds the Krebs cycle; the space outside it holds the protons.
bio-mitochondrion.alt: A schematic mitochondrion: a rounded double boundary, an outer and an inner membrane, with the inner one folded back and forth into cristae. The folding is the point, because it gives the inner membrane far more area than the outer one, and that membrane carries the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so more area means more ATP can be made. The fluid enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix, where the Krebs cycle runs; it has the lower proton concentration and the higher pH. The narrow region between the two membranes holds the high proton concentration. The difference between those two regions is the gradient that drives ATP synthase. Illustrative data.

bio-dna-antiparallel.title: DNA: two strands, paired and antiparallel
bio-dna-antiparallel.subtitle: Each base pairs with one partner, and the two strands run opposite ways
bio-dna-antiparallel.caption: The two sugar-phosphate backbones run in opposite directions: read left to right the top strand goes 5' to 3', and the bottom strand goes 3' to 5'. Between them each base is joined to its one partner by hydrogen bonds — two for A with T, three for C with G.
bio-dna-antiparallel.alt: A short stretch of DNA drawn flat, as a ladder rather than as a helix. The two sides of the ladder are the sugar-phosphate backbones, two strands of nucleotides, and each carries an arrowhead showing its direction from the 5' end to the 3' end. The arrowheads point opposite ways: the top strand's 3' end is on the right and the bottom strand's 3' end is on the left, which is what antiparallel means. The rungs are the base pairs. Each base on one strand is joined to exactly one base on the other: adenine always with thymine, cytosine always with guanine. The joins are hydrogen bonds, drawn as dashes, and there are two of them in every A with T pair and three in every C with G pair, so the C with G pairs are held together more strongly. bio-fluid-mosaic.entry_title: Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane
bio-fluid-mosaic.title: The plasma membrane: a bilayer with things embedded in it
bio-fluid-mosaic.subtitle: Phosphate heads face the water; tails face each other; the rest is embedded
bio-fluid-mosaic.caption: The phospholipids form two leaflets: the hydrophilic phosphate heads face the watery surroundings on both sides and the hydrophobic tails face each other in the interior. Proteins, steroids such as cholesterol, glycoproteins and glycolipids sit within that framework, and the carbohydrate chains are all on the outside face.
bio-fluid-mosaic.alt: A cross-section of a plasma membrane. Two rows of small circles are the phosphate heads of the phospholipids; the upper row faces the extracellular fluid and the lower row faces the cytoplasm, because both are watery and the heads are hydrophilic. From each head two lines run inward: these are the hydrophobic fatty acid tails, and the tails of the two rows meet in the middle, away from the water. Embedded in this framework are several other things. Two proteins cross the whole bilayer, so their hydrophobic regions are in contact with the fatty acids while their ends reach the water on each side. A small block sitting among the tails and reaching neither surface is a steroid, cholesterol in vertebrate animals. One of the crossing proteins and one single lipid head carry branched chains of sugars drawn above the membrane, making them a glycoprotein and a glycolipid; both carbohydrate chains are on the extracellular face, never the cytoplasmic one. All of these components move within the plane of the membrane, which is what the word fluid in fluid mosaic refers to. Illustrative data.
bio-fluid-mosaic.note: Heads to the water, tails to each other; the sugar chains are all on the outside face.

chem-electrochemical-cell.title: Reading a galvanic cell diagram
chem-electrochemical-cell.subtitle: Oxidation at the anode; electrons through the wire; ions through the bridge
chem-electrochemical-cell.caption: Each part of the diagram answers one question. The electrodes say where each half-reaction happens — oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. The solutions hold the active species. The meter in the external circuit reads the cell potential. The salt bridge lets ions move between the half-cells so neither builds up a charge.
chem-electrochemical-cell.alt: A galvanic cell. Two beakers each hold a half-cell solution containing the active species of one half-reaction, and an electrode dips into each solution. The left electrode is the anode, where oxidation occurs; the right electrode is the cathode, where reduction occurs. Which electrode changes mass, or evolves a gas, depends on the half-reactions, and this diagram names neither. A wire runs from the top of one electrode to the top of the other, and a meter sits in that external circuit to read the cell potential. Electrons travel through that wire in one direction only, from the anode to the cathode, shown by an arrow above the wire. An inverted U shaped salt bridge joins the two solutions: both of its ends are below the liquid surface, and it touches neither electrode. Ions move through it, cations toward the cathode and anions toward the anode, which keeps each half-cell electrically neutral and lets the current keep flowing. Illustrative data.
chem-electrochemical-cell.note: Electrons go anode to cathode through the wire; ions go through the bridge.
